system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and history of gastrojejunal anastomotic ulcers (medically treated with resolution) was admitted for persistent nausea/vomiting with poor oral intake and protein-calorie malnutrition while dependent on TPN via a tunneled right internal jugular catheter. She underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic gastrostomy tube placement on 2170-01-16. A postoperative gastrografin study confirmed correct tube position, after which tube feeds (Fibersource HN) were initiated and advanced without worsening baseline nausea; TPN was discontinued on postoperative day 1. By hospital day 3 she reached goal nocturnal cycled tube feeds (80 mL/hr for 12 hours), tolerated a stage V diet in small amounts, and home services were arranged for tube feeding support. With stable enteral nutrition, Interventional Radiology removed the tunneled catheter without complication, and she was discharged home ambulatory and stable with tube care instructions, residual checks, return precautions, and continuation of an oral proton pump inhibitor with surgical follow-up.

Date of Birth:  ___             Sex:   F

No Known Allergies / Adverse Drug Reactions
 
Attending: ___.
 
Chief Complaint:
Dry heaves
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
___: EGD

 
History of Present Illness:
___ with very complicated recent medical history.  She is s/p 
gastric bypass in ___, which was complicated by anastomotic 
ulcers.  Her ulcers and pain were so severe as to require 
placement of a ___ catheter for high-dose PPI and TPN, as 
well as a G-tube for nutrition.  Her ___ catheter was 
removed earlier this year, and her G-tube was removed ___ at 
her request.  Since the removal of her G-tube, she has been 
having progressively more abdominal pain, dry heaving, and 
inability to take adequate nutrition.  She was initially having 
dry heaves a few times a week, but is now having them many times 
per day.  She has not had any regurgitation, and has been having 
normal bowel movements, without diarrhea, blood, or melena.  She 
was seen in clinic on ___, at which time she was started on 
Carafate and given a small prescription for dilaudid.  She was 
also scheduled for upper endoscopy to evaluate the anastomosis 
for ___.  She called the office today complaining of continued 
pain and concern that she was not getting adequate nutrition.

 
Past Medical History:
PMH: GERD, PCOS, G-J anastomitic ulcer, h/o C. diff colitis ___

PSH: R carpal tunnel surgery ___, R shoulder surgery ___, 
tubal ligation ___, lap RNY gastric bypass ___, R IJ Hickman 
catheter ___ (removed), appendectomy, lap G-tube placement ___ 
(removed)

___

Her family history remarkable for obesity and CAD

Creat-0.8 Na-141 K-3.6 Cl-103 HCO3-29 AnGap-13 

___: EGD:
-Evidence of previous roux-en-y gastric by pass was noted. 
-A small erosion was seen in the cardia of the gastric remnant. 
-The blind limb appeared unremarkable. 
-The alimentary limb and the jejuno-jejunal anastomosis appeared 
unremarkable
 
Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ presented to the Emergency Department on ___ due to complaints of worsening dry heaves and concern 
regarding her ability to consume adequate nutrition.  
Intravenous fluids including a banana bag were administered and 
the patient was transferred to the general surgical ward once 
deemed stable. 

On hospital day 2, the patient's vital signs remained stable and 
she was able to tolerate a stage 4 bariatric diet without 
incident.  Additionally, she was voiding adequately.  She was 
also given intravenous protonix BID.  On hospital day 3, an 
upper endoscopy was performed, which was essentially normal 
except for a small erosion noted in the gastric pouch. 

At the time of discharge on hospital day 4, the patient was 
doing well, afebrile with stable vital signs.  The patient was 
tolerating a stage 5 diet, ambulating, voiding without 
assistance, and pain was well controlled.  She will continue 
oral pantoprazole and sucralfate.  The patient also received 
pain medication for the next week. The patient received 
discharge teaching and follow-up instructions with understanding 
verbalized and agreement with the discharge plan.  
 
Medications on Admission:
Sucralfate 1 gram QID
Citalopram 40 mg daily
Metoclopramide 10 mg BID
Temazepam 15 mg q HS
Aripiprazole 20 mg daily
Pantoprazole 40 mg daily
 
Discharge Medications:
1. sucralfate 1 gram Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO QID (4 times 
a day).  
2. citalopram 20 mg Tablet Sig: Two (2) Tablet PO DAILY (Daily). 
 
3. lorazepam 1 mg Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO BID (2 times a 
day) as needed for anxiety.  
4. metoclopramide 10 mg Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO BID (2 
times a day) as needed for nausea.  
5. temazepam 15 mg Capsule Sig: Two (2) Capsule PO HS (at 
bedtime).  
6. aripiprazole 10 mg Tablet Sig: Two (2) Tablet PO DAILY 
(Daily).  
7. pantoprazole 40 mg Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) Sig: One 
(1) Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) PO twice a day.  

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Gastric erosion

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital with complaints of dry 
heaving.  An upper endoscopy was performed --------.  You are 
now preparing for discharge to home with the following 
instructions:

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:
*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.
*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.
*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.
*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.
*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.
*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.
*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.
*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.
*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.
Please resume all regular home medications , unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.
Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids. Avoid lifting 
weights greater than ___ lbs until you follow-up with your 
surgeon.
Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.
Incision Care:
*Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner if you have 
increased pain, swelling, redness, or drainage from the incision 
site.
*Avoid swimming and baths until your follow-up appointment.
*You may shower, and wash surgical incisions with a mild soap 
and warm water. Gently pat the area dry.
*If you have staples, they will be removed at your follow-up 
appointment.
*If you have steri-strips, they will fall off on their own. 
Please remove any remaining strips ___ days after surgery.

 
Followup Instructions:
___

diagnoses.long_title: Other complications of other bariatric procedure
Other specified procedures as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I hear you’ve been having worsening dry heaves and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been nonstop. I’m dry heaving many times a day now. I’m scared I’m not getting any nutrition in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. Since your G-tube was removed, have you been able to keep down any liquids or soft foods at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Very little. I try, but then the pain and heaving start. I’m not really vomiting food—just retching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood when you vomit or in your stool? Any black, tarry stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. My bowel movements have been normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any diarrhea, fevers, or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and prior anastomotic ulcers, we want to make sure there isn’t a new ulcer or narrowing at the connection. We’ll start with IV fluids tonight to treat dehydration and help your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried this is happening because I had the tube removed. Did I mess things up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You didn’t do anything wrong. Sometimes symptoms return after changes in how nutrition is supported, and sometimes irritation or reflux can flare. Our job now is to stabilize you and look for a treatable cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you giving me in the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fluids, and we’re also planning a vitamin-containing infusion—often called a banana bag—because people with poor intake can get depleted. We’ll also check labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. First we’ll see if we can get you comfortable and tolerating a bariatric diet again. We’ll also plan an upper endoscopy to look at the pouch and connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was started on Carafate in clinic. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—sucralfate, or Carafate, coats irritated areas. We’ll continue it here, and we’ll also increase acid suppression while you’re inpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My reflux has been awful too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with what you’re describing. We’ll give pantoprazole through the IV twice a day for now, which is stronger and faster than pills when you’re not keeping things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still having waves of pain. Can I have something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll treat pain, but we’ll do it carefully because stronger pain meds can worsen nausea. We’ll aim for the lowest effective dose and reassess often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after the fluids and medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still dry heaving, but not as constant. I’m exhausted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it eased some. Your vital signs have been stable. We’re going to start you on a stage 4 bariatric diet today—very gentle, small amounts—and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does stage 4 mean again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a soft, more advanced bariatric diet than clear liquids, but still easy to digest. The key is tiny portions, slow sips, and stopping before you feel full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I start heaving again, does that mean something is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not automatically. Dry heaving can come from irritation, reflux, or sensitivity after bypass. The endoscopy will help us rule out a narrowing or ulcer at the connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down a little of the diet, but I’m scared to push it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right approach—don’t push. The goal today is tolerance without triggering symptoms. You’re also urinating well, which tells us hydration is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When is the scope happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning it for tomorrow. You’ll need to be NPO—nothing by mouth—for a period beforehand. The team will give you exact timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. What are you looking for exactly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll look at the gastric pouch and the small intestine limbs created by the bypass, including the connections. We’re checking for ulcers, erosions, inflammation, or narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Today is the endoscopy day. How are your symptoms right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some pain, but less. The dry heaves are less frequent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the IV pantoprazole going. After the procedure, we’ll decide whether to switch back to pills and advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable and usually don’t remember much. It’s done through the mouth with a camera; no incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the endoscopy. It went smoothly. Want to hear what we found?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. Is there an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The good news is the bypass anatomy looked as expected. The blind limb looked unremarkable, and the alimentary limb and the jejuno-jejunal connection looked unremarkable. We did see a small erosion in the cardia area of the gastric remnant/pouch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a big ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—this was described as a small erosion, not a large ulcer, and there was no mention of a blockage. That fits with irritation and reflux-type symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes an erosion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often acid exposure and irritation. After bariatric surgery, the anatomy changes and the lining can be more sensitive. That’s why we’re focusing on strong acid suppression and sucralfate to protect the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart with your bariatric diet and advance as tolerated. Start slow. If you can keep it down without worsening symptoms, that’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the dry heaves will come back when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid worry. We’ll send you home on pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day. We’ll also give you metoclopramide to use as needed for nausea, and a short course of pain medication for the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pantoprazole twice a day—wasn’t I on it once a day before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Given the erosion and your symptoms, we’re increasing it to twice daily to better control acid and help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you do overnight with eating and drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I had small amounts and didn’t dry heave as much. Pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re tolerating a stage 5 bariatric diet now, you’re walking around, and you’re urinating without trouble. Those are the main discharge goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What is stage 5 compared to stage 4?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stage 5 is a step up—more regular textured bariatric foods, still focusing on small portions and avoiding anything that triggers reflux or discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My labs—are they okay? I’m always worried about being malnourished again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated in the past by anastomotic ulcers presented with worsening abdominal pain and frequent dry heaves after prior removal of her gastrostomy tube, with concern for inadequate nutrition. She was stabilized with IV fluids including a vitamin-containing infusion and treated with IV pantoprazole twice daily while her diet was cautiously advanced; she tolerated a stage 4 bariatric diet and maintained stable vital signs and urine output. On hospital day 3 she underwent upper endoscopy, which showed expected post-bypass anatomy with unremarkable limbs and jejuno-jejunal anastomosis and only a small gastric erosion. By discharge she was tolerating a stage 5 bariatric diet, ambulating independently, and had controlled pain; she was discharged home on oral pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate with as-needed antiemetic and short-term pain medication, along with return precautions and surgical follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this stay were overall reassuring—kidney function and electrolytes looked stable, and your blood counts were acceptable though on the lower side earlier. The bigger issue is making sure you can maintain intake at home, and we’ll give you clear return precautions if you can’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking all my other meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your regular home medications unless we specifically changed them. The key changes are pantoprazole now twice daily and continuing sucralfate. Metoclopramide is as needed for nausea, and lorazepam is as needed for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back if you can’t keep down fluids or medications, if you feel dehydrated—dry mouth, fast heartbeat, dizziness when standing—if you vomit blood or see black stools, if you have worsening pain, chest symptoms, shortness of breath, or fever over 101.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drive myself home if I’m taking pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—don’t drive or operate machinery while taking pain medication. Arrange a ride today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to avoid lifting or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—avoid heavy lifting until you follow up with your surgeon. Also rest, walk several times a day, and focus on hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the plan is just meds and diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Since the endoscopy didn’t show a blockage and only a small erosion, the treatment is medical: acid suppression with pantoprazole twice daily, mucosal protection with sucralfate, and careful bariatric diet progression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I feel better knowing it wasn’t something severe. I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll finalize your discharge paperwork now and make sure you understand the medication schedule and follow-up instructions before you leave.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated in the past by anastomotic ulcers presented with worsening abdominal pain and frequent dry heaves after prior removal of her gastrostomy tube, with concern for inadequate nutrition. She was stabilized with IV fluids including a vitamin-containing infusion and treated with IV pantoprazole twice daily while her diet was cautiously advanced; she tolerated a stage 4 bariatric diet and maintained stable vital signs and urine output. On hospital day 3 she underwent upper endoscopy, which showed expected post-bypass anatomy with unremarkable limbs and jejuno-jejunal anastomosis and only a small gastric erosion. By discharge she was tolerating a stage 5 bariatric diet, ambulating independently, and had controlled pain; she was discharged home on oral pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate with as-needed antiemetic and short-term pain medication, along with return precautions and surgical follow-up.
